courses.title: CARSI Structural Drying Practitioner
courses.description:
The credential course for the CARSI Structural Drying Practitioner designation, produced for restoration technicians and supervisors in Australia and New Zealand who dry water-damaged buildings, and for assessors and insurance-support staff who need to judge a drying job. It builds measured field judgement; it does not replace a manufacturer’s instructions, a Safety Data Sheet or a site’s own rules.

Six modules take you from the first visit to a defensible drying file: the drying job and the dry standard, including the asbestos check before any cut; psychrometry in g/kg that proves drying is happening; evaporation and air-mover placement, with the mould and contamination hold rules; refrigerant, LGR and desiccant dehumidification, with water removal calculated in litres per day; closed, open and heat-assisted drying systems, 230 V / 10 A power budgets and the Australian and New Zealand electrical-safety rules; and daily monitoring, documentation and a whole-job case study. Every lesson has a worked metric example, a diagram, a field tool and a sources list. A practical task and a 20-question designation exam complete the designation.

Australian and New Zealand law is stated side by side where it differs: WHS laws and the HSWA 2015, asbestos dates and licences, testing and tagging, consumer guarantees and notifiable events. Aligned to the principles in ANSI/IICRC S500:2025, cited by name only.

CARSI Structural Drying Practitioner is a CARSI Southern Hemisphere Restoration Designation.
courses.shortDescription: The credential course for the CARSI Structural Drying Practitioner designation, for Australia and New Zealand: the dry standard, psychrometry in g/kg, evaporation and airflow, dehumidifier selection and litres-per-day checks, 230 V/10 A power and electrical safety, and the drying file.

modules.title: Module 1: The Drying Job and the Dry Standard

lessons.title: What a structural drying practitioner does
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification in the evidence ledger.

On the job

A washing-machine hose fails in the laundry of a 1980s brick-veneer home in Parramatta while the owners are at work. By the time they get home, water has crossed the laundry and the hallway, soaked into the timber-look laminate and wicked about 300 mm up the plasterboard. The insurer sends you. Nobody on site is asking whether you can set up machines; they are asking whether the house will be dry, how long it will take, and how you will prove it.

The idea

Structural drying is the controlled removal of water from a building’s materials — framing, sheet linings, floors, slabs and cavities — back to a measured dry standard, without causing secondary damage on the way. Wet materials swell, delaminate, corrode and support microbial growth over hours and days, so time matters. A practitioner does four things a machine cannot: measures, decides, verifies and documents.

This course follows a seven-stage arc. Assess and make safe: isolate power to wet areas, identify hazards and the water source. Set the dry standard: take reference readings from unaffected materials. Plan: choose the evaporation, dehumidification and heat you need, and budget the power. Set up. Monitor every visit. Adjust when the numbers say the plan is not working. Verify and document when every material reaches its dry standard.

The duty to do this safely sits with the business. In Australia, a person conducting a business or undertaking (PCBU) holds the primary duty of care under the model Work Health and Safety laws, which apply in every jurisdiction except Victoria, where the Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004 applies. In New Zealand, section 36 of the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 (HSWA) places the same primary duty on the PCBU, so far as is reasonably practicable. Both countries rank controls the same way: eliminate the risk first, then substitute, isolate or engineer it out, with administrative controls and personal protective equipment (PPE) last. New Zealand writes that order into regulation 6 of the Health and Safety at Work (General Risk and Workplace Management) Regulations 2016.

Before you cut, check for asbestos. Structural drying often means removing skirting, cutting flood lines in plasterboard or lifting floor coverings. In Australia, buildings built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos; in New Zealand, WorkSafe advises that any building built or renovated before 2000 could contain it. You cannot tell by looking. In both countries a licence is needed to remove more than 10 m² of non-friable asbestos, and the ACT does not allow homeowners or tradespeople to remove any amount themselves. If the house might contain asbestos, sample before you cut.

Common first-visit mistakes. Setting up machines before the power to wet areas is isolated. Cutting plasterboard in a pre-1990 Australian or pre-2000 New Zealand building before anyone has thought about asbestos. Forgetting to size the loss in square metres, so the equipment plan and the power budget are guesses. Leaving the job without a single reference reading, so nobody can later say what dry means for this house. Each one is cheap to avoid on day one and expensive to fix on day five.

This course is aligned to the principles in ANSI/IICRC S500:2025, cited by name only.

See it

The CARSI drying arc. Monitoring and adjusting form a loop that repeats every visit until the materials reach their dry standard.

Do it in metric

Size the Parramatta loss before you plan anything. The wet floor runs 3.2 m × 2.6 m = 8.32 m². The wet wall is the room perimeter, 2 × (3.2 + 2.6) = 11.6 m, less a 0.8 m doorway = 10.8 m, wicked to 0.3 m: 10.8 × 0.3 = 3.24 m² of plasterboard. Record both areas on the start sheet; they drive the equipment plan in Module 4 and the power budget in Module 5.

Field download

The Drying job start and dry-standard sheet walks the first visit: make-safe, the asbestos check (pre-1990 Australia, pre-2000 New Zealand), loss size in m², and the reference readings you will take in the next lesson.

Check yourself

The Module 1 check asks you to order the drying arc, name the duty holder in Australia and New Zealand, and decide when to stop for an asbestos check. Each answer explains the reasoning a supervisor would expect.

Takeaway

Structural drying is measured work: assess, set the dry standard, plan, set up, monitor, adjust, verify and document. The PCBU carries the safety duty in both countries, and an asbestos check comes before the first cut. Next: setting the dry standard.

Sources for this lesson

  • Safe Work Australia, Duties of a PCBU. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Safe Work Australia, Model WHS laws. Read 02/11/2026.
  • WorkSafe Victoria, Occupational Health and Safety Act and regulations. Read 02/11/2026.
  • New Zealand Legislation, Health and Safety at Work Act 2015, section 36. Read 02/11/2026.
  • SafeWork NSW, Class B asbestos removal licence. Read 02/11/2026.
  • WorkSafe New Zealand, Asbestos in Aotearoa New Zealand. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Asbestos and Silica Safety and Eradication Agency, Householders and home renovators. Read 02/11/2026.
  • New Zealand Legislation, Health and Safety at Work (Asbestos) Regulations 2016, regulation 56. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Setting the dry standard and the drying goal
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification in the evidence ledger.

On the job

Day three in Parramatta. The owner asks, “Is it dry yet?” One technician says the meter reads “green”; another says the laminate “feels dry”. Neither answer would survive a question from the insurer’s assessor. The question has a defensible answer only if you wrote down, on day one, what dry looks like for each material in this house.

The idea

A dry standard is the moisture reading a material shows when it is in balance with its normal surroundings. You find it by measuring the same material in an unaffected part of the same building — a bedroom floor, an internal wall away from the water — with the same meter on the same scale. The drying goal is to bring each wet material back to its reference. Houses differ by climate, season and construction, so a reference taken on the day beats any number from memory: timber in a Darwin wet season sits wetter than timber in a Canberra winter.

Know what your meter is telling you. A pin (resistance) meter measures between two electrodes driven into the material; a timber scale reads moisture content (%MC) directly for the species it is set for. A pinless (capacitance or impedance) meter reads a zone below the surface without damage, but density, metal fixings and surface water affect it. Many meters show a relative scale for plasterboard, masonry and concrete; a relative number is only comparable with another reading of the same material on the same meter. That is why the reference must match the material.

Record every reading with its location, material, meter, scale, date and time, on a numbered sketch. A reading without its scale is not evidence. Take references before you set up equipment, because running air movers changes the house you are measuring.

Moisture content for timber is measured on an oven-dry basis: the mass of water divided by the mass of the dry wood. That makes it possible to work out how much water a piece of timber has to lose.

See it

The dry standard comes from the same material in an unaffected part of the same building, read with the same meter on the same scale.

Do it in metric

A 1.20 kg offcut of hallway flooring reads 24 %MC; the bedroom reference reads 11 %MC. The dry mass is 1.20 ÷ 1.24 = 0.968 kg. At the dry standard the piece would weigh 0.968 × 1.11 = 1.074 kg. So this one offcut must lose 1.20 − 1.074 = 0.126 kg, about 126 mL of water. Multiply that across 8.32 m² of floor and the dehumidifier in Module 4 has real work to do.

Field download

Use the reference-readings table on the Drying job start and dry-standard sheet: one row per material, with the unaffected reading, meter, scale and location beside the affected reading.

Check yourself

The Module 1 check asks you to choose a valid reference, explain why a relative reading cannot be compared across materials, and work the oven-dry moisture arithmetic.

Takeaway

Dry is a number you set on day one: the same material, unaffected, same meter, same scale. Record every reading with its scale. Next (Module 2): the psychrometric readings that prove drying is happening.

Sources for this lesson

  • USDA Forest Products Laboratory, Wood Handbook, chapter 12: Drying and control of moisture content. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: The four numbers: temperature, RH, dew point and g/kg
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification in the evidence ledger.

On the job

A Brisbane technician records 80 %RH on day one and 55 %RH on day two and writes “drying well”. But the house was 20 °C on day one and 26 °C on day two, because the owner turned the air-conditioning off. Was any water actually removed? From RH alone, nobody can tell.

The idea

Four numbers describe moist air. Temperature (°C) is the dry-bulb reading. Relative humidity (RH, %) is how close the air is to saturation at that temperature. The Bureau of Meteorology puts the trap plainly: relative humidity is not a measure of the actual amount of moisture, because it depends on the air temperature. Warm the same air and its RH falls, although not one gram of water has left the room.

The dew point (°C) is the temperature to which air must be cooled for dew to form. It rises as the air carries more water. The humidity ratio is the mass of water vapour per kilogram of dry air, in grams per kilogram (g/kg). It does not change when the air warms or cools, so it is the number to compare between rooms, between days and across a dehumidifier. (You may see imperial “grains per pound” on imported equipment: 1 g/kg = 7 grains per pound.)

You do not need to do the maths on site. A thermo-hygrometer gives temperature and RH; a psychrometric chart, calculator or app turns them into dew point and g/kg. What you must do is log g/kg, because a falling g/kg is evidence that water is leaving the air, and a falling RH on its own is not.

A practical habit: take the four numbers in the same places at the same height every visit, after the meter has settled in that air for a minute or two.

Common mistakes. Writing down RH and nothing else. Comparing a reading taken next to a heater with one taken in a cold corner. Reading the thermo-hygrometer the moment you walk in from a hot van, before it has settled. Quoting imported grains per pound without converting to g/kg. And reporting “humidity is down” to an assessor when the only change was that the room warmed up.

See it

Relative humidity changes with temperature; grams of water per kilogram of dry air does not. Log g/kg to compare readings.

Do it in metric

Test the Brisbane readings. Day one, 20 °C at 80 %RH = 11.7 g/kg (dew point 16.4 °C). Day two, 26 °C at 55 %RH = 11.6 g/kg (dew point 16.3 °C). The air holds almost exactly the same water; the RH fell because the room warmed. The other direction works the same way: Parramatta’s wet laundry at 22 °C and 75 %RH holds 12.4 g/kg, and warmed to 26 °C with no water removed, the same 12.4 g/kg would read about 59 %RH. “Drying well” needs the g/kg to fall.

Field download

The Psychrometric daily log has columns for °C, %RH, dew point and g/kg at each reading point, so the g/kg trend is visible at a glance.

Check yourself

The Module 2 check asks you to say which number proves water removal, convert a reading pair to the right conclusion, and define dew point.

Takeaway

RH moves with temperature; g/kg and dew point move with water. Log g/kg every visit. Next: where to take the readings and what they prove.

Sources for this lesson

  • Bureau of Meteorology, Definitions for 9am and 3pm statistics. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Reading the job: g/kg depression and the condensation check
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification in the evidence ledger.

On the job

Day two in Parramatta. The dehumidifier is humming and the bucket line is draining, but the owner wants to know whether the machine is “doing anything”. A second question is quieter: the laundry slab feels cold, and the tiles in the corner are sweating. Both questions have answers in the same set of readings.

The idea

Take the four numbers at five points every visit: outside, an unaffected room, the affected room, the dehumidifier inlet and its outlet. Convert each to g/kg and read them as a set.

  • Outlet below inlet shows the dehumidifier is removing water from the air passing through it. The difference is the g/kg depression; the larger it is, the more water per kilogram of air the unit is pulling out.
  • Affected above unaffected shows the wet materials are still loading the air with evaporated water. As drying proceeds, the affected g/kg should trend down towards the unaffected reading.
  • Outside is context, not proof. It tells you whether opening a window would help or hurt (Module 5).

Then run the condensation check. Air cooled to its dew point produces condensation, so any surface colder than the room’s dew point — a slab on ground, an external wall in winter, a cold-water pipe, the window in a Hobart or Dunedin morning — can collect water while you are trying to dry the room. Measure the surface temperature with an infrared thermometer or a surface probe and compare it with the dew point. If the surface is colder, lower the room’s g/kg, raise the surface temperature, or both, before you trust any reading on that surface.

Write the five readings in the same order every time. A drying log is a trend, and a trend is only as good as its consistency.

See it

Five readings every visit. The dehumidifier outlet must be lower than its inlet, and the affected room should trend down towards the unaffected room.

Do it in metric

The Parramatta readings: outside 16 °C, 85 %RH = 9.6 g/kg; unaffected bedroom 22 °C, 50 %RH = 8.2 g/kg; affected laundry 22 °C, 70 %RH = 11.6 g/kg; dehumidifier inlet the same 11.6 g/kg; outlet 30 °C, 30 %RH = 7.9 g/kg. The depression is 11.6 − 7.9 = 3.7 g/kg: the unit is working. The laundry is still 3.4 g/kg above the bedroom, so evaporation is still loading the air. Condensation check: if the laundry reaches 24 °C and 60 %RH, its dew point is 15.8 °C; the slab measures 14 °C, so it sits below the dew point and the sweating tiles are condensation, not a new leak.

Field download

The Psychrometric daily log lays out the five points in order, with a depression box (inlet minus outlet) and a condensation-check row (surface °C against room dew point).

Check yourself

The Module 2 check asks you to work a g/kg depression, interpret affected against unaffected, and decide whether a cold surface is at risk of condensation.

Takeaway

Five points, every visit, in g/kg. Outlet below inlet proves the dehumidifier works; affected trending to unaffected proves the job is drying; a surface below dew point is a condensation risk. Next (Module 3): how water leaves a wet material.

Sources for this lesson

  • Australian Building Codes Board, Condensation in buildings handbook (2023). Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: How wet materials give up water
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification in the evidence ledger.

On the job

Two jobs in the same Melbourne week. In a Footscray unit, wet carpet and underlay are dry in two days. In a Box Hill house, a concrete slab under floating floorboards is still reading high on day six, with the same equipment and the same weather. The equipment did not fail. The materials are different, and they give up water differently.

The idea

Evaporation is water changing from liquid to vapour at a surface. Three things drive it.

A vapour pressure difference. Water vapour moves from where its partial vapour pressure is higher to where it is lower. A warm wet surface has a high vapour pressure; dry room air has a low one. The bigger the difference, the faster vapour leaves the surface. That is why dehumidification (lowering the room’s g/kg) and heat (raising the surface’s vapour pressure) both speed drying.

Air movement at the surface. Right at a wet surface sits a thin layer of still, nearly saturated air. Vapour has to cross it. Moving air across the surface thins that layer and carries the vapour away, which is the job of an air mover.

Energy. Evaporating water takes heat — about 2.45 megajoules for every kilogram near room temperature. That heat comes from the air and the material, so evaporation cools a wet surface. A cold room or a cold slab evaporates slowly because there is little energy to draw on.

Materials behave differently because of where the water sits. Water on the surface and in large pores, as in carpet, underlay and the face of plasterboard, leaves quickly. Water held deep inside dense materials such as concrete, masonry and hardwood has to travel to the surface first, and once the surface dries the rate falls away. Dense materials are the long pole on most jobs, and some, such as a wet slab under a floating floor, cannot dry until the covering is lifted or the slab is opened to the air.

Common mistakes. Expecting a slab to dry at the same rate as the carpet above it. Adding airflow to a covered material that the air cannot reach. Running a cold house without heat in winter and wondering why nothing moves. Forgetting that evaporation cools the surface, so a wet wall can read colder than the air around it. List your slow materials on day one and plan for them first.

See it

Evaporation needs a vapour pressure difference, air movement at the surface and energy. Remove any one and drying slows.

Do it in metric

How much energy does drying need? Suppose the Box Hill slab and framing hold 10 L of water above their dry standard. Ten litres is 10 kg, and 10 kg × 2.45 MJ/kg = 24.5 MJ. Divided by 3.6 MJ per kWh, that is about 6.8 kWh of heat just to turn the water into vapour, before any losses. It explains why a cold house in July dries more slowly than the same house in February.

Field download

The Air-mover placement and material check starts with a material list: mark each wet material as fast (surface and open pores) or slow (dense or covered), so the slow ones get attention first.

Check yourself

The Module 3 check asks you to name the three drivers of evaporation, explain why a dense or covered material dries slowly, and work the energy arithmetic.

Takeaway

Evaporation needs a vapour pressure difference, moving air at the surface and energy. Dense and covered materials dry last. Next: placing air movers, and when to hold them back.

Sources for this lesson

  • Australian Building Codes Board, Condensation in buildings handbook (2023). Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Placing air movers, and when not to
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification in the evidence ledger.

On the job

An Adelaide technician sets four air movers in the middle of a wet lounge room, all pointing at the centre. The carpet in the middle dries; the wet wall bases and the corners, where the water sat longest, barely move. On day three the skirting is still wet and the plaster has started to blister. The machines were there. The airflow was not where the water was.

The idea

An air mover does one job: it moves air across a wet surface to thin the still layer and carry vapour away. Placement decides whether it does that job on the materials that matter.

  • Put the airflow on the wet surface. Angle air movers along the base of wet walls so the air sweeps the wall and the floor beside it. Work around the room in one direction, so each air mover’s flow feeds the next instead of fighting it.
  • Cover all of the wet surface, including corners, behind doors and under kitchen kickboards, which hold water longest.
  • Open what is covered. Air cannot reach a wet slab under a floating floor or water inside a wall cavity until you lift the covering, remove skirting or open small holes behind it. Check for asbestos first (Module 1).
  • Match air movers to dehumidification. Airflow lifts water into the air; if the dehumidifier cannot keep up, the room’s g/kg rises and drying stalls. Module 4 shows how to check.

How many air movers, and at what spacing, comes from the drying method your business works to and the plan your supervisor signs off; the count follows the wet area and how hard each material is to dry.

The hold rules. If visible mould is present, do not run air movers: high airflow across mouldy surfaces spreads spores through the building. Dry with dehumidifiers and air filtration under containment until remediation is done, and when in doubt, treat suspected mould as mould. Do the same where contaminated (Category 3) water has left debris: airflow would spread the contamination. Mould remediation is its own CARSI course, the CARSI Mould Remediation Practitioner.

See it

Angle air movers along the wet wall bases so airflow sweeps the wet surfaces. Hold them back where mould or contamination would be spread.

Do it in metric

Imported air movers are often rated in cubic feet per minute (CFM). Convert to metric before you plan: 1 CFM = 1.699 m³/h, so a unit rated at 2,000 CFM moves 2,000 × 1.699 = about 3,400 m³/h. Write the metric figure on the job plan. For a sense of scale, a 4.0 m × 3.5 m room with a 2.4 m ceiling holds 33.6 m³ of air; that one unit moves about a hundred times that volume every hour, which is why the room’s g/kg climbs fast if the dehumidifier is undersized.

Field download

The Air-mover placement and material check has a placement sketch grid, the CFM-to-m³/h conversion, and the two hold rules to tick before any air mover is switched on.

Check yourself

The Module 3 check asks you to correct a poor placement, convert an imported airflow rating, and apply the mould and contamination hold rules.

Takeaway

Put the airflow where the water is, open what is covered, and keep dehumidification in step. No air movers over visible mould or contaminated debris. Next (Module 4): dehumidification.

Sources for this lesson

  • SafeWork NSW, Class B asbestos removal licence. Read 02/11/2026.
  • WorkSafe New Zealand, Asbestos in Aotearoa New Zealand. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Refrigerant, LGR and desiccant: how each removes water
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification in the evidence ledger.

On the job

A Dunedin crew dries a flooded basement in July with the same refrigerant dehumidifier that worked well in a Gold Coast job in January. In Dunedin the bucket line barely drips and the coil has a skin of ice. The unit is not faulty. It is working outside the conditions it removes water well in.

The idea

Refrigerant dehumidifiers draw room air over a coil kept colder than the air’s dew point. Water vapour condenses on the coil and drains away, and the air is reheated across the hot side of the refrigeration circuit before it leaves, which is why the outlet is warmer and drier than the inlet. The catch is temperature: when the air is cold, the coil has to run colder still to get below the dew point, and its surface can fall below freezing. Ice then forms on the coil and water removal drops.

Low grain refrigerant (LGR) units are refrigerant dehumidifiers designed to keep removing water when the air is already fairly dry, so they can pull a room’s g/kg lower than a conventional unit. They are still refrigerant machines, and the same cold-weather limit applies.

Desiccant dehumidifiers pass the air through a slowly turning wheel coated with a material that attracts water vapour. A separate, heated reactivation air stream dries the wheel and carries the water away as warm, wet air, which must be ducted out of the drying zone, usually outside the building. Because desiccants do not rely on a cold coil, they keep working when the air is cold or already very dry; desiccant dehumidification can continue even when the dew point of the air is below freezing.

Choose by conditions. Warm, humid jobs — most of Queensland and the Northern Territory, and Australian summers generally — suit refrigerant and LGR units. Cold jobs — Tasmania, Canberra and alpine areas, and much of New Zealand in winter, from Christchurch and Dunedin to Queenstown — often need a desiccant, heat, or both. Whatever you choose, buy and hire units built for 230 V, 50 Hz supply and sold through Australian or New Zealand distributors, and read the rating plate before you plug in.

Common mistakes. Blaming a refrigerant unit for low output in a cold basement instead of checking the dew point. Venting desiccant reactivation air back into the drying zone, which returns the water to the room. Leaving a refrigerant unit iced overnight. Choosing equipment by what is in the van rather than by the conditions in the house.

See it

Refrigerant units condense water on a cold coil; desiccant units adsorb it. Conditions on the job decide which works better.

Do it in metric

Check whether a refrigerant unit can work. The affected room is at 24 °C and 60 %RH, so its dew point is 15.8 °C: the coil must be colder than 15.8 °C to condense anything, which is easy. Now take a Dunedin basement at 12 °C and 85 %RH: the dew point is 9.6 °C, so the coil must run below 9.6 °C, close enough to freezing that icing is likely. That is the point to consider a desiccant or to add heat first.

Field download

The Dehumidifier selection and performance card starts with a conditions check: room °C, %RH and dew point, then a refrigerant, LGR or desiccant decision, with the reactivation-ducting reminder for desiccants.

Check yourself

The Module 4 check asks you to explain how each type removes water, why refrigerant output falls in cold air, and which type suits a cold winter job.

Takeaway

Refrigerant and LGR units condense water on a cold coil and slow down in cold air; desiccants adsorb water and keep working when it is cold. Duct desiccant reactivation air outside. Next: proving a dehumidifier is working, in litres per day.

Sources for this lesson

  • Hawaii Natural Energy Institute, University of Hawaii, Desiccant dehumidification literature and technology review. Read 02/11/2026.
  • McGahey and Harriman, Desiccants: benefits for the second century of air-conditioning (Texas A&M repository). Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Proving a dehumidifier works: litres per day from g/kg
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification in the evidence ledger.

On the job

An assessor on a Perth job questions the dehumidifier hire charge: “How do I know that machine took any water out?” The technician points to the rated capacity on the box. The assessor is not persuaded, and rightly so: a rating is measured at the maker’s test conditions, not in this house today.

The idea

You can calculate how much water a dehumidifier is removing from your own readings. Three numbers are needed:

  • the unit’s process airflow in m³/h (from the specification sheet, converted from CFM if necessary);
  • the density of air, about 1.2 kg/m³ at room temperature near sea level;
  • the g/kg depression, inlet minus outlet, from your psychrometric readings.

Water removed (kg/h) = airflow (m³/h) × 1.2 (kg/m³) × depression (g/kg) ÷ 1000. One kilogram of water is one litre, so multiply by 24 for litres per day. The result is an estimate, but it is your estimate from this job, and anyone can check the arithmetic.

Use it three ways. Prove performance: record the calculated litres per day in the drying log. Cross-check: compare it with the condensate actually pumped or emptied. A big mismatch points to a blocked filter, a restricted outlet, a leaking pump line or a misread meter. Watch the trend: as the room dries, the inlet g/kg falls, the depression narrows and the daily litres drop. That fall is expected and is good evidence that drying is nearing its end, provided the materials are approaching their dry standard too.

Sizing is a planning decision, made from the wet area, the materials and the conditions, and confirmed by these readings on the first return visit. If the calculated removal cannot keep up with the water the air movers are lifting, the room’s g/kg climbs; add dehumidification or reduce airflow until the numbers balance.

See it

Water removed = airflow × air density × g/kg depression. Cross-check the result against the condensate log.

Do it in metric

The Parramatta unit has a process airflow of 340 m³/h and a depression of 3.7 g/kg. Air through the unit: 340 × 1.2 = 408 kg/h. Water removed: 408 × 3.7 ÷ 1000 = 1.51 kg/h, and × 24 = about 36 L/day. Two days later the depression is 2.0 g/kg: 408 × 2.0 × 24 ÷ 1000 = about 20 L/day. The fall is expected as the house dries. A desiccant unit on a cold job, at 500 m³/h taking air from 7.4 to 3.0 g/kg: 500 × 1.2 × 4.4 × 24 ÷ 1000 = about 63 L/day.

Field download

The Dehumidifier selection and performance card has the litres-per-day calculation laid out line by line, with a box for the logged condensate so the cross-check happens every visit.

Check yourself

The Module 4 check asks you to calculate litres per day from airflow and depression, explain a falling daily figure, and act on a mismatch with the condensate log.

Takeaway

Airflow × 1.2 × g/kg depression, × 24 ÷ 1000, gives litres per day. Log it, cross-check it, and expect it to fall as the job dries. Next (Module 5): drying systems and power.

Sources for this lesson

  • Hawaii Natural Energy Institute, University of Hawaii, Desiccant dehumidification literature and technology review. Read 02/11/2026.
  • McGahey and Harriman, Desiccants: benefits for the second century of air-conditioning (Texas A&M repository). Read 02/11/2026.

modules.title: Module 5: Drying Systems, Power and Electrical Safety in Australia and New Zealand

lessons.title: Closed, open and heat-assisted drying systems
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification in the evidence ledger.

On the job

Three jobs, three answers. In Alice Springs in October, a technician opens the windows and drying speeds up. In Townsville in February, a technician does the same and the house gets wetter. In Christchurch in June, opening up dries the air but chills the house so much that evaporation almost stops. Same idea, three outcomes. The outside readings decide.

The idea

Drying systems fall into three working patterns.

Closed (contained) drying. Shut the drying zone off from outside and from the rest of the building — doors closed, polythene sheeting where needed — and let the dehumidifiers remove the water. A smaller, sealed volume reaches a low g/kg faster and keeps the dry air where the wet materials are. This is the default for most Australian and New Zealand jobs.

Open drying (air exchange). Bring outside air in and push humid inside air out. It helps only when the outside air has a lower g/kg than the inside air and is warm enough that it does not chill the materials and slow evaporation. Dry inland Australia often passes that test; the humid tropics and coast in summer usually fail it.

Heat-assisted drying. Adding heat raises the vapour pressure at wet surfaces and supplies the energy evaporation needs (Module 3), so it is most useful in cold conditions. Use electric heat with a power budget (next lesson) and keep the dehumidifier capacity up, or the warm air simply fills with water. Never run fuel-burning heaters, generators or petrol-powered equipment inside: they produce carbon monoxide, which has no colour, smell or taste and can kill. Australian product-safety guidance says never to use gas or kerosene heaters or petrol or diesel generators inside a house or in a poorly ventilated area, and WorkSafe New Zealand lists space heaters and oil or gas heaters among carbon monoxide sources. New Zealand sets a workplace exposure standard for carbon monoxide of 20 ppm averaged over 8 hours; in Australia, check the current Safe Work Australia exposure limit.

Many jobs end up as a combination: closed and dehumidified overnight, with heat, and opened briefly when the outside air is genuinely drier and warm. Record the readings that justified each choice.

Common mistakes. Opening windows because “fresh air dries things” without comparing g/kg. Leaving doors to the rest of the house open, so the dehumidifier is drying the whole building instead of the wet zone. Adding heat without enough dehumidification, so the warm air fills with water. And, most dangerous of all, bringing a gas heater or a generator inside to save time.

See it

Choose the system from the outside g/kg and temperature against the inside readings. Fuel-burning heaters never go inside.

Do it in metric

Inside the wet zone: 22 °C, 70 %RH = 11.6 g/kg. Alice Springs outside, 32 °C at 28 %RH = 8.3 g/kg: drier and warm, so air exchange helps. Townsville outside, 29 °C at 75 %RH = 19.0 g/kg: far wetter, so stay closed. Christchurch outside, 9 °C at 90 %RH = 6.4 g/kg, against an inside 18 °C at 65 %RH = 8.4 g/kg: drier, but at 9 °C it would chill the house. Closed drying with electric heat and a desiccant is usually the better plan there.

Field download

The Power and electrical safety worksheet (AU/NZ) opens with a drying-system decision box: inside g/kg, outside g/kg and outside °C, and the system chosen, with the carbon monoxide rule printed beside it.

Check yourself

The Module 5 check asks you to choose a system from outside and inside readings, explain why cold outside air can slow drying, and apply the carbon monoxide rule.

Takeaway

Closed is the default; open only when outside g/kg is lower and the air is warm enough; heat helps in the cold but must be electric. No fuel-burning equipment indoors. Next: the power budget and electrical safety.

Sources for this lesson

  • ACCC Product Safety Australia, Carbon monoxide safety. Read 02/11/2026.
  • WorkSafe New Zealand, Dangers of carbon monoxide. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: 230 V power budgets and electrical safety in Australia and New Zealand
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification in the evidence ledger.

On the job

A Hamilton technician plugs a dehumidifier, four air movers and an air scrubber into a double GPO in the hallway and a power board in the lounge. Both outlets are on the same circuit. At 1 am the breaker trips and the job sits idle until morning. In a wet house, a tripped circuit is the good outcome; the bad outcome is an overheated lead or a shock.

The idea

Supply is the same on both sides of the Tasman. Australian supply is nominally 230 V at 50 Hz, and New Zealand’s standard low voltage is a nominal 230 V at 50 Hz. The standard outlet is a 10 A general power outlet (GPO). One 10 A circuit can supply about 230 V × 10 A = 2300 W in total, and several GPOs in a room often share one circuit breaker. Overload it and the breaker cuts the power, which stops the drying, often unnoticed overnight.

Budget before you plug in. Read each machine’s current draw in amps from its rating plate. Add them per circuit and keep each total comfortably below the circuit rating, because motors and compressors draw a surge at start-up. Find which GPOs share a circuit by checking the switchboard labels or with the owner, and spread the load. Some larger desiccants and heaters carry a 15 A plug, with a wider earth pin, which will not fit a 10 A GPO: use a 15 A outlet or a suitable supply. Never modify a plug or force an adaptor.

Electrical safety in Australia. Portable electrical equipment and extension leads at a workplace must be protected by a residual current device (RCD, or safety switch); a workplace RCD on a socket outlet up to 20 A trips at no more than 30 mA. Equipment used in hostile conditions such as a wet building must be regularly inspected and tested by a competent person, and inspection, testing and tagging guidance sits in AS/NZS 3760:2022.

Electrical safety in New Zealand. The rules differ. Under the Electricity (Safety) Regulations 2010, in-service appliances and leads must be RCD-protected in certain circumstances, such as damp conditions — which describes every wet job. WorkSafe New Zealand states that testing and tagging is not mandatory: what is legally required is that equipment is electrically safe and maintained in a safe condition. Testing and tagging to AS/NZS 3760 is an option for a business to show it complies. On a drying job, an RCD on every lead, a visual check of every cord and plug each visit, and a tagging regime are good practice in both countries.

Generators. Never run a generator indoors, including in an internal garage, in either country. Place it outside, away from openings.

See it

One 10 A circuit at 230 V supplies about 2300 W. Split the load, use RCD protection, and follow your country’s inspection and testing rules.

Do it in metric

Budget the Hamilton hallway. LGR dehumidifier 4.5 A, four air movers at 1.2 A, one air filtration device at 2.0 A (illustrative draws; read the rating plates). All on one circuit: 4.5 + 4.8 + 2.0 = 11.3 A, over the 10 A rating before any start-up surge. Even without the air filtration device, 9.3 A leaves almost no headroom. Split: circuit A, dehumidifier + two air movers = 4.5 + 2.4 = 6.9 A (about 1590 W); circuit B, two air movers + air filtration device = 2.4 + 2.0 = 4.4 A (about 1010 W). Both run through RCD protection.

Field download

The Power and electrical safety worksheet (AU/NZ) totals amps per circuit, flags any circuit above 8 A for a second look, and carries the Australian and New Zealand RCD and testing checklists side by side.

Check yourself

The Module 5 check asks you to total a circuit, split an overloaded one, and state where the Australian and New Zealand testing rules differ.

Takeaway

230 V, 50 Hz, 10 A GPOs in both countries: budget amps per circuit and split the load. RCD-protect everything on a wet job. Australia requires inspection and testing of equipment in hostile conditions; New Zealand requires safe equipment and treats tagging as one way to show it. Next (Module 6): monitoring and documentation.

Sources for this lesson

  • NSW Government, Voltage optimisation fact sheet. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Ausgrid, Electricity Safety: Electrical equipment. Read 02/11/2026.
  • New Zealand Legislation, Electricity (Safety) Regulations 2010. Read 02/11/2026.
  • New Zealand Legislation, Electricity (Safety) Regulations 2010, regulation 29. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Electrical Safety Office Queensland, Safety switches. Read 02/11/2026.
  • WorkSafe ACT, Residual current devices. Read 02/11/2026.
  • SafeWork NSW, Electrical inspection and testing. Read 02/11/2026.
  • SafeWork SA, Inspection and testing of electrical equipment. Read 02/11/2026.
  • WorkSafe New Zealand, Testing and tagging electrical appliances. Read 02/11/2026.
  • WorkSafe New Zealand, Ensuring safety of plug-in electrical appliances. Read 02/11/2026.

modules.title: Module 6: Monitoring, Documentation and the Whole Job

lessons.title: Daily monitoring, the drying log and when to change the plan
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification in the evidence ledger.

On the job

A Townsville house in February. Day one to day two, the plasterboard readings fall well. Day two to day three, the slab under the floating floor does not move at all. One technician adds two more air movers. The room’s g/kg climbs and the house feels sticky. The log had the answer, but it was read as a list of numbers instead of a trend.

The idea

Monitor every visit, the same way. Read each numbered point on the moisture map with the same meter and scale as day one; take the five psychrometric readings; calculate the dehumidifier depression and litres per day; check equipment, power and RCDs; and note what changed. Plot or tabulate material readings against the dry standard so the trend is obvious.

Read the trend, then diagnose.

  • Materials falling, air g/kg falling: the plan is working. Leave it alone.
  • Air g/kg not falling, or rising: evaporation is outrunning dehumidification, or outside air is getting in. Check the depression, seal the zone, or add dehumidification. More air movers will make it worse.
  • Air dry, but a material not moving: the water is bound deep or covered. Add heat, focus airflow on that surface, or open it up — lift the floating floor, remove the skirting — after the asbestos check.
  • A cold surface below dew point: condensation, not drying. Lower g/kg or warm the surface.

Change one thing at a time and write down why, so the next reading tells you whether the change worked.

Common mistakes. Taking readings at different points each day, so there is no trend to read. Using a different meter on day three. Adding equipment by habit when the readings call for a different change. Declaring the job dry because the air is dry while a slab is still above its reference. Leaving the reason for a change in someone’s head instead of in the file.

The drying file is the job’s evidence. Keep the start sheet, the dry standards, the moisture map, every day’s log, photos with dates, the equipment and power plan, any change and the reason for it, and the final readings showing each material at its dry standard. That file is what answers the assessor, the owner and, if it comes to it, a dispute. Consumers in Australia receive automatic guarantees under the Australian Consumer Law, including that services are carried out with due care and skill; New Zealand’s Consumer Guarantees Act 1993 gives a guarantee that services are carried out with reasonable care and skill. A complete drying file is how you show both.

If someone is hurt. In New Zealand a PCBU must notify WorkSafe as soon as possible after becoming aware of a notifiable event, and a death is reported immediately on 0800 030 040. In Australia, follow your state or territory WHS regulator’s notification process.

See it

A stall in the log is a decision point. Diagnose it, change one thing, and record why.

Do it in metric

The Townsville log. Inside, day one 27 °C at 62 %RH = 13.9 g/kg; day three 27 °C at 50 %RH = 11.1 g/kg. Outside 29 °C at 75 %RH = 19.0 g/kg, so the house stays closed. The plasterboard reached its dry standard on day four. The slab sat at the same reading from day two to day three; the floating floor was lifted on day three, and the slab began to fall. The invoice shows labour and equipment in AUD with GST at 10 % added: a A$2,400 ex-GST drying charge becomes A$2,400 × 1.10 = A$2,640 including GST.

Field download

The Daily drying log and completion checklist has one row per visit for material points, five psychrometric readings, depression and litres per day, a trend column, and a “change made and why” box.

Check yourself

The Module 6 check asks you to diagnose a stalled log, choose the right single change, and state what the drying file must contain.

Takeaway

Monitor the same way every visit, read the trend, diagnose a stall, change one thing and record why. The drying file is the evidence of care and skill in both countries. Next: the whole job, start to finish.

Sources for this lesson

  • New Zealand Legislation, Consumer Guarantees Act 1993, section 28. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Australian Taxation Office, How GST works. Read 02/11/2026.
  • WorkSafe New Zealand, What events need to be notified?. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Whole-job case study: a Christchurch winter loss
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification in the evidence ledger.

On the job

A burst pipe in the ceiling of a 1978 weatherboard house in Christchurch runs overnight in late June. Water has come through the lounge ceiling, soaked the carpet and underlay, wetted two internal plasterboard walls and pooled on the timber floor near the hallway. Outside it is 9 °C at 90 %RH. The house has been unheated for a day and reads 12 °C at 85 %RH inside. You are the practitioner on the job.

The idea

Day one: assess and make safe. Isolate power to the wet ceiling and lounge circuits and check for sagging ceiling linings before anyone works under them. The house was built in 1978, before 2000, so it may contain asbestos: textured ceilings and older linings are suspects, and you cannot tell by looking. Arrange sampling before any lining is cut and treat suspect material as asbestos until results return. Under HSWA the business’s primary duty applies from the first minute. Obtain the safety data sheet for any antimicrobial or chemical you bring on site, as New Zealand’s hazardous-substances rules require, and keep the National Poisons Centre number, 0800 764 766, on the job sheet (in Australia, the Poisons Information Centre is 13 11 26).

Set the dry standard. Take references from the same materials in the unaffected bedrooms: timber floor, plasterboard and carpet, same meter, same scale. Map the wet areas on a numbered sketch.

Plan. Cold air is the problem. At 12 °C a refrigerant unit’s coil would run close to freezing, so the plan is closed drying with electric heat and a desiccant, reactivation air ducted outside. Outside air is drier but would chill the house, so the windows stay shut. Lift the wet carpet and underlay, which cannot be dried in place economically, and set air movers along the wet wall bases. Budget the power: heaters and the desiccant go on separate circuits, everything RCD-protected because the house is damp.

Days two to four: monitor and adjust. The heat lifts the lounge to 20 °C. The log shows the air g/kg falling and the plasterboard moving, but the timber floor near the hallway stalls on day three. The diagnosis: the boards are cupped and the water is held deep in the timber; the change is to focus airflow and heat on that floor, and nothing else, and record why.

Days five and six: verify, document and hand over. Every mapped point reaches its reference reading. The file holds the asbestos results, references, daily logs, depression and litres-per-day calculations, the power plan, photos, the day-three change and the final readings. The owner receives a plain-English summary of what was wet, what was done and how dryness was proved: the evidence of reasonable care and skill under the Consumer Guarantees Act 1993.

Your designation. The CARSI Structural Drying Practitioner designation is awarded on two pieces of evidence: the practical task, where you plan and evidence a drying job of your own or the supplied one, graded against a five-part rubric; and the final designation exam at the end of this module.

See it

The whole job on one line. Every decision on it is backed by a reading in the drying file.

Do it in metric

The Christchurch numbers. Inside on arrival, 12 °C at 85 %RH = 7.4 g/kg, dew point 9.6 °C. After heating, the lounge reads 20 °C at 60 %RH = 8.7 g/kg, dew point 12.0 °C: the g/kg rose because heat drove evaporation, which is the point. The desiccant moves 500 m³/h and takes air from about 7.4 to 3.0 g/kg on day two: 500 × 1.2 × 4.4 × 24 ÷ 1000 = about 63 L/day. The air target is the unaffected bedroom, 20 °C at 45 %RH = 6.5 g/kg.

Field download

Finish with the completion section of the Daily drying log and completion checklist: every mapped point against its reference, the change record, the owner summary and the sign-off.

Check yourself

The Module 6 check asks you to sequence the case study’s first-day decisions, justify the drying system, and say what proves the job is finished. The final designation exam follows.

Takeaway

The whole job is the arc from Module 1, run on readings: make safe and check for asbestos, set the dry standard, choose the system from the conditions, budget the power, monitor and adjust one thing at a time, and prove dry in the file.
